hook: Bats are not blind.
facts: People say blind as a bat, but every kind of bat can see.
Many use sound to hunt in the dark, but they also use their eyes.
Some big fruit bats see better than humans when the light is low.

hook: Lightning often strikes the same place twice.
facts: People say lightning never strikes the same place twice.
But lightning loves tall, pointed things, and it hits them again and again.
The Empire State Building is hit around twenty times every year.

hook: The ten percent brain idea is a myth.
facts: Many people believe we only use one tenth of our brain.
Brain scans show that almost every part is active during a normal day.
Even when you sleep, no area of your brain stays completely off.

hook: Nails do not keep growing after death.
facts: An old story says hair and nails keep growing in the grave.
In truth, the body dries out after death, and the skin shrinks back.
That makes nails and hair look longer, even though they have not grown at all.

hook: Swallowed gum does not stay inside for years.
facts: Kids are told that gum stays in your stomach for seven years.
Your body cannot break gum down, that part is true.
But it simply moves through you like other food, and leaves in a few days.

hook: Sugar does not make children hyper.
facts: Many parents are sure that sugar makes kids go wild.
In studies, children got sugar or a fake sweetener, and nobody knew which.
There was no difference, but parents who thought their kid had sugar saw a wilder child.

hook: Toilets do not spin the other way in Australia.
facts: People say water drains the other way south of the equator.
The spin of the Earth does turn giant storms, but it is far too weak for a sink.
The direction only depends on the shape of the toilet and how the water goes in.

hook: The Bermuda Triangle is not more dangerous.
facts: The Bermuda Triangle is famous for ships and planes that vanish.
But it is also one of the busiest pieces of ocean in the world.
Insurance companies do not charge more to cross it, because accidents there are normal.

hook: Sherlock Holmes never said elementary, my dear Watson.
facts: It is the most famous line linked to the great detective.
But in all the original stories, that exact line never appears.
It came later, from films and plays that added it.

hook: Darth Vader never says Luke, I am your father.
facts: It is one of the most quoted movie lines ever.
In the film, Luke shouts that Vader killed his father.
Vader simply answers: No, I am your father.

hook: Frankenstein is not the monster's name.
facts: In the book by Mary Shelley, Victor Frankenstein is a young scientist.
He builds a creature from dead body parts and brings it to life.
The creature never gets a name, and Mary Shelley was only eighteen when she started the story.

hook: The Olympic torch relay is not ancient.
facts: Many think the torch relay goes back to ancient Greece.
The old games did keep a sacred fire burning, but nobody ran with it.
The first relay was held in nineteen thirty-six, for the games in Berlin.

hook: Coffee beans are not beans.
facts: Coffee grows on bushes as small red fruits called coffee cherries.
Inside each fruit there are usually two seeds.
Those seeds are dried and roasted, and we call them beans.

hook: Guinea pigs are not pigs, and not from Guinea.
facts: Guinea pigs come from the Andes mountains in South America.
They are rodents, much closer to mice than to any pig.
Nobody is sure about the name, but they do squeal a bit like tiny pigs.

hook: Killer whales are actually dolphins.
facts: Orcas are the biggest members of the dolphin family.
Like other dolphins, they breathe through a hole on top of their head and hunt in teams.
When orcas arrive, even great white sharks swim away.

hook: Hyenas are closer to cats than to dogs.
facts: Hyenas look and act a lot like wild dogs.
But their family tree tells a very different story.
They belong to the same big group as cats, mongooses and lions.

hook: The original panda is red.
facts: The red panda was called a panda decades before the black and white one.
The giant panda got the name later, because both of them eat bamboo.
And the two animals are not even close relatives.

hook: Panama hats are made in Ecuador.
facts: The famous straw hats are woven by hand in Ecuador.
In the eighteen hundreds, they were shipped through Panama and sold to miners and canal workers.
When an American president wore one at the Panama Canal, the wrong name stuck forever.

hook: Kiwi fruit is not from New Zealand.
facts: The fuzzy fruit first grew wild in China, where it was called the Chinese gooseberry.
Farmers in New Zealand started growing it in the nineteen hundreds.
To sell it abroad, they renamed it after their national bird, the kiwi.

hook: Most Brazil nuts come from Bolivia.
facts: Brazil nut trees grow wild in the Amazon rainforest.
They almost never grow on farms, because they need one special kind of bee.
Today, the country that sells the most Brazil nuts is Bolivia.

hook: Nutella started as a loaf you sliced.
facts: After World War Two, chocolate was rare and expensive in Italy.
A baker named Pietro Ferrero mixed a little cocoa with lots of cheap hazelnuts.
At first it was a solid block that you cut with a knife and put on bread.

hook: Carbonara is younger than the Second World War.
facts: Many people think it is an ancient Roman recipe.
But it first appears in writing only after nineteen forty-four.
One theory says it was made with eggs and bacon from American army supplies.

hook: Tiramisu is younger than your grandparents.
facts: It feels like an old family recipe from Italy.
But it only became known in the nineteen sixties and seventies, in the north east of Italy.
The name means pick me up, thanks to all the coffee and sugar.

hook: Cotton candy was invented by a dentist.
facts: In eighteen ninety-seven, a dentist and a candy maker built a machine together.
It spun hot melted sugar into very thin threads.
They sold it at the World's Fair in nineteen oh four, and it was a huge hit.

hook: Mr Potato Head once came without a potato.
facts: When the toy came out in nineteen fifty-two, it was just a set of plastic parts.
Children had to push the eyes, nose and mouth into a real potato.
The plastic potato body was only added years later.

hook: The Netherlands has more bikes than people.
facts: The country is very flat, and its cities were built for cycling.
There are about twenty-three million bikes for eighteen million people.
Every year, thousands of bikes are fished out of the canals in Amsterdam.

hook: The French horn is actually German.
facts: The modern horn was developed mostly in Germany in the eighteen hundreds.
English speakers called it French, maybe because early hunting horns came from France.
Most musicians around the world just call it the horn.

hook: Arabic numbers were invented in India.
facts: The ten number symbols we use were first developed in India.
Arab scholars learned them and spread them across the Middle East.
Europeans then learned them from Arab books, so they called them Arabic.

hook: Chinese checkers is not from China.
facts: The game was invented in Germany in the eighteen nineties, under another name.
American sellers renamed it Chinese checkers to make it sound exotic.
And it is not even a kind of checkers.

hook: In Denmark, Danish pastries are called Vienna bread.
facts: In the eighteen hundreds, bakers in Denmark went on strike.
The bakeries hired workers from Austria, who brought their own recipes.
So the Danes still call these pastries Vienna bread.

hook: The turkey bird is named after a country.
facts: Turkeys come from North America, not from Turkey.
English traders mixed them up with an African bird that was sold through Turkey.
And in Turkey, the bird is called hindi, which means from India.

hook: Spaghetti and meatballs is not really Italian.
facts: In Italy, small meatballs are usually eaten on their own, not on pasta.
Italian families in America could buy far more meat than back home.
So they made the meatballs bigger and put them on spaghetti, and a new dish was born.

hook: Japanese tempura came from Portugal.
facts: In the fifteen hundreds, Portuguese sailors and priests arrived in Japan.
On holy days when they could not eat meat, they fried fish and vegetables in batter.
The Japanese loved it, and the name may come from the Latin word for those holy days.

hook: Fried fish came to Britain with Portuguese Jews.
facts: Centuries ago, Jewish families fled Portugal and Spain and settled in England.
They fried fish on Friday, so they could eat it cold on the day of rest.
Later it met chips, and became Britain's most famous meal.

hook: Every Granny Smith apple comes from one tree.
facts: If you plant an apple seed, the new tree gives very different apples.
So farmers copy good trees by joining their branches onto new roots.
Every Granny Smith comes from one tree found by a woman in Australia in the eighteen sixties.

hook: Orange was a fruit before it was a color.
facts: Before the fruit reached England, there was no word for that color.
People just called it yellow red.
That is why we say redhead, and not orangehead.

hook: In English, pineapple first meant pine cone.
facts: Hundreds of years ago, English people called pine cones pineapples.
When explorers found the tropical fruit, it looked like a giant pine cone.
So the name moved to the fruit, and the cones got a new name.

hook: The word muscle means little mouse.
facts: Muscle comes from the Latin word musculus.
It means little mouse.
The Romans thought a muscle moving under the skin looked like a mouse running.

hook: The word disaster means bad star.
facts: Long ago, people believed the stars controlled their lives.
Dis means bad, and astro means star.
So when something terrible happened, they blamed a bad star.

hook: A clue was once a ball of thread.
facts: In old English, a clew was a ball of yarn.
In a Greek myth, a hero used a ball of thread to find his way out of a maze.
So following a clue meant following the thread out of a problem.

hook: OK started as a joke about bad spelling.
facts: In the eighteen thirties, newspapers in Boston loved silly short forms.
O K stood for oll korrect, a funny way to misspell all correct.
The joke was forgotten, but the word went around the world.

hook: Avocado comes from an old word for testicle.
facts: Avocados grew in Mexico long before Europeans arrived.
The Aztecs called the fruit ahuacatl.
The same word also meant testicle, maybe because of the way the fruit hangs in pairs.

hook: Stomach rumbling has an official name.
facts: That noise your belly makes is called borborygmi.
It is gas and liquid being squeezed through your gut.
It happens all the time, but it is loudest when your stomach is empty.

hook: One hill's name has eighty-five letters.
facts: In New Zealand there is a small hill with a Maori name.
The name tells the story of a man who played his flute there for the one he loved.
With eighty-five letters, it is the longest place name in the world.

hook: One cash machine speaks Latin.
facts: Vatican City is the smallest country in the world.
Its official language is still Latin.
So its cash machines let you choose Latin on the screen.

hook: Reno is farther west than Los Angeles.
facts: Los Angeles sits on the Pacific coast of California.
But the coast of California bends to the east as it goes south.
So Reno, in the desert of Nevada, is actually farther west.

hook: The Hundred Years War was not a hundred years.
facts: It was a long fight between England and France.
It started in thirteen thirty-seven and ended in fourteen fifty-three.
That is one hundred and sixteen years, and it was really many wars with long breaks.

hook: Greenland is icy, and Iceland is quite green.
facts: Greenland is almost completely covered by a giant sheet of ice.
Iceland has green fields and a milder climate than its name suggests.
An old story says Erik the Red chose the name Greenland to attract settlers.

hook: A moment was once exactly ninety seconds.
facts: In the Middle Ages, an hour was split into smaller parts.
One of those parts was called a moment.
It lasted about ninety seconds, so just a moment was a real measure of time.

hook: Dog days are named after a star, not dogs.
facts: The hottest weeks of summer are called the dog days.
In ancient times, they came when Sirius, the Dog Star, rose together with the Sun.
People believed the star added its own heat to the Sun's.

hook: Russia once had a tax on beards.
facts: In sixteen ninety-eight, Tsar Peter the Great came back from a trip to Europe.
He wanted Russian men to look modern, and that meant no beards.
Men who kept their beard had to pay a tax and carry a token to prove it.

hook: Britain once had a tax on windows.
facts: In sixteen ninety-six, England taxed houses by the number of windows they had.
To pay less, many people filled their windows with bricks.
You can still see bricked up windows on old buildings today.

hook: Horses can sleep standing up.
facts: Horses can lock their legs in place, so they do not fall over.
This lets them doze while standing, ready to run from danger.
But for deep sleep they must lie down, just for a short time each day.

hook: The Moon has earthquakes too.
facts: Astronauts left instruments on the Moon to listen for shaking.
They found moonquakes, some caused by the pull of the Earth.
Some lasted more than ten minutes, because the dry rock rings like a bell.

hook: The and symbol was once part of the alphabet.
facts: Children used to recite the alphabet with one more sign at the end.
They said: X, Y, Z, and per se and.
Said fast, it turned into ampersand, the name we still use today.

hook: China is huge but uses only one time zone.
facts: China is almost as wide as the whole United States.
Before nineteen forty-nine it had several time zones.
Now everyone follows Beijing time, so in the far west the sun can rise at ten in the morning.

hook: You could once rent an entire country.
facts: Liechtenstein is a tiny country between Switzerland and Austria.
Around two thousand and eleven, it was offered for rent on a booking website.
Guests could have castles, their own street signs, and even their own money.

hook: Iceland has no army at all.
facts: Iceland is a real country, but it has no soldiers of its own.
It has a coast guard and police, and its allies help protect it.
Even its police officers almost never carry guns.

hook: Iceland has an app to avoid dating cousins.
facts: Iceland has fewer than four hundred thousand people, and many are related.
A family tree database there goes back more than a thousand years.
Two people can bump their phones, and the app warns them if they are close family.

hook: Japan has more pets than children.
facts: Fewer babies are born in Japan every year.
At the same time, more people live alone with cats and dogs.
Today there are more pet cats and dogs in Japan than children under fifteen.

hook: A Japanese train company apologized for leaving early.
facts: In twenty seventeen, a train near Tokyo left the station too soon.
It was not minutes early, only twenty seconds.
The company still said sorry for the trouble it may have caused.

hook: One country officially measures its happiness.
facts: Most countries judge success by how much money they make.
Bhutan, a small kingdom in the Himalayas, decided that was not enough.
It measures Gross National Happiness, and checks people's health, nature and free time.

hook: One country's flag shows a modern rifle.
facts: Mozambique won its independence after a long war.
Its flag shows an open book, a farming tool, and a rifle.
The rifle stands for the fight that made the country free.

hook: London Bridge now stands in Arizona.
facts: In the nineteen sixties, the old London Bridge was slowly sinking into the river.
An American businessman bought it and shipped it across the ocean, stone by stone.
It was rebuilt in a desert town in Arizona, where it still stands today.

hook: Ancient Rome had a tax on urine.
facts: Roman laundries used urine to clean clothes.
Emperor Vespasian put a tax on collecting it from public toilets.
When his son complained, he held up a coin and said that money does not smell.

hook: In ancient Egypt, killing a cat meant death.
facts: Egyptians believed cats were linked to the goddess Bastet.
Even killing one by accident could be punished by death.
When a family cat died, people shaved their eyebrows to show their sadness.

hook: Ancient Egyptians had a pregnancy test using grain.
facts: A woman would pee on small bags of wheat and barley seeds.
If the seeds grew, she was thought to be pregnant.
Modern scientists tested it, and it worked most of the time.

hook: Ancient Rome had fast food restaurants.
facts: Many Romans lived in small apartments with no kitchen.
So they bought hot food at street counters called thermopolia.
In Pompeii, archaeologists found one with food still inside the pots.

hook: Aristotle thought the brain was for cooling blood.
facts: The great Greek thinker believed the heart was the center of thought.
He thought the brain was just there to keep the blood cool.
Egyptian embalmers also threw the brain away, but carefully kept the heart.

hook: Left and right shoes were once the same.
facts: For a long time, most shoes were made perfectly straight.
You could wear either shoe on either foot.
Shoes shaped for left and right only became normal in the eighteen hundreds.

hook: A dog found the stolen World Cup trophy.
facts: In nineteen sixty-six, the trophy was stolen in London, months before the tournament.
A week later, a dog named Pickles was sniffing a bush on a walk.
He found it wrapped in old newspaper, and became a national hero.

hook: Lobsters were once food for prisoners.
facts: In early America, lobsters washed up on beaches in huge piles.
They were so cheap that they were fed to servants and prisoners.
Today, the same animal is one of the most expensive things on a menu.

hook: The fire hydrant patent burned in a fire.
facts: The fire hydrant was invented in America in the early eighteen hundreds.
Its patent was kept in the Patent Office in Washington.
In eighteen thirty-six, the Patent Office burned down, and the hydrant patent burned with it.

hook: One inventor's ashes were turned into frisbees.
facts: Ed Headrick designed the modern frisbee and invented disc golf.
Before he died, he made one last request.
His ashes were mixed into plastic and made into discs for his family and friends.

hook: Super glue was discovered while making gun sights.
facts: In World War Two, scientists wanted clear plastic for gun sights.
They found a liquid that stuck to everything it touched, so they threw it away.
Years later, one of them realized that was the point, and super glue went on sale.

hook: Tissues were first made for gas masks.
facts: In World War One, a soft cotton-like material was made for gas mask filters.
After the war, the company had tons of it left over.
They sold it to remove makeup, and then people started blowing their noses in it.

hook: A wrong part led to the first pacemaker.
facts: In the nineteen fifties, an engineer was building a machine to record heartbeats.
He grabbed the wrong part and put it into the circuit.
It started sending regular pulses, just like a heartbeat, and the pacemaker was born.

hook: X-rays were discovered by accident.
facts: In eighteen ninety-five, a German scientist was testing a glass tube with electricity.
A screen across the room started to glow, even though the tube was covered.
He put his wife's hand in front of it, and they saw her bones.

hook: A dropped flask led to safety glass.
facts: In nineteen oh three, a French scientist dropped a glass flask.
It cracked, but it did not break into pieces.
A plastic liquid had dried inside and held it together, and safety glass was born.

hook: Non-stick pans came from a failed experiment.
facts: In nineteen thirty-eight, a chemist was trying to make a new cooling gas.
He opened a container and it looked empty, but it was too heavy.
Inside was a white, slippery coating, which became the non-stick layer on pans.

hook: A chemist found sweetener on his dirty hands.
facts: In eighteen seventy-nine, a chemist worked late with coal tar chemicals.
At dinner, he noticed that his bread tasted strangely sweet.
The taste came from his unwashed hands, and the first artificial sweetener was found.

hook: Seven Up once contained a mood drug.
facts: The drink was launched in nineteen twenty-nine.
It contained lithium, a substance later used as a medicine for mood.
It was taken out in the late nineteen forties, and nobody knows what the name means.

hook: Amazon was almost called Cadabra.
facts: When the company started in nineteen ninety-four, its name was Cadabra.
A lawyer heard it on the phone and thought it was cadaver, a dead body.
So the founder chose the name of the biggest river in the world.

hook: Apple's first logo showed Isaac Newton.
facts: In nineteen seventy-six, the company's logo was a detailed drawing.
It showed Newton sitting under a tree, with an apple about to fall.
It was soon replaced by the simple apple with a bite.

hook: You helped scan old books without knowing.
facts: Those wavy words you typed to prove you were human had a second job.
One of the words came from old books and newspapers that computers could not read.
Millions of people typing them turned whole archives into digital text.

hook: Tetris was made in the Soviet Union.
facts: In nineteen eighty-four, a computer scientist in Moscow built a simple puzzle game.
It spread from computer to computer, and then across the world.
For years the creator earned nothing from it, because the state owned it.

hook: Mario was first called Jumpman.
facts: In nineteen eighty-one, he appeared in Donkey Kong as a carpenter.
He got a mustache and a cap because tiny pixels could not show a mouth or hair.
His real name came from the landlord of the company's office in America.

hook: A Game Boy survived a bombing and still works.
facts: During the Gulf War, a soldier's Game Boy was badly burned.
Its plastic case melted and turned black.
But when it was turned on, it still played Tetris, and it was shown in a store in New York.

hook: Pac-Man was inspired by a pizza.
facts: The game's designer was eating a pizza with one slice missing.
The shape gave him the idea of a round hero with a big mouth.
He later said the story was only half true, but it stuck anyway.

hook: The first song played in space was Jingle Bells.
facts: In December nineteen sixty-five, two astronauts were circling the Earth.
They told mission control they had seen a strange object, like a sleigh.
Then they played Jingle Bells on a tiny harmonica they had sneaked on board.

hook: America's anthem uses the tune of a drinking song.
facts: The words were written in eighteen fourteen, during a battle.
The music came from an older British song, sung at a gentlemen's club.
The club was a group of friends who met to drink and sing.

hook: Beethoven wrote his most famous symphony while deaf.
facts: Beethoven started losing his hearing in his late twenties.
When he wrote his Ninth Symphony, he was almost completely deaf.
At the first show, a singer had to turn him around so he could see the crowd cheering.

hook: Young Bach walked hundreds of kilometers to hear music.
facts: In seventeen oh five, Bach was a young church organist in Germany.
He walked about four hundred kilometers to hear a famous organist play.
He was given a few weeks off, but stayed away for around four months.

hook: The Thinker was first called The Poet.
facts: Rodin first made the statue for a giant gate, based on a story about hell.
The man on top was meant to be the poet Dante, looking down at the souls below.
Later it was shown alone, and people gave it a new name: The Thinker.

hook: Volleyball was invented to be gentler than basketball.
facts: Basketball was invented in eighteen ninety-one, in Massachusetts.
A sports teacher nearby thought it was too rough for older businessmen.
So he mixed tennis and handball, and first called his game mintonette.

hook: Hockey pucks are frozen before every game.
facts: A rubber puck bounces a lot when it is warm.
So in pro hockey, pucks are kept in a freezer before the game.
Frozen pucks slide smoother and bounce less on the ice.

hook: Your fingers have no muscles.
facts: You can move your fingers fast and with great control.
But the muscles that move them are in your palm and your arm.
They pull the fingers with long tendons, like strings on a puppet.

hook: Your eyes see the world upside down.
facts: The lens in your eye works like a camera lens.
It flips the image, so it lands upside down at the back of your eye.
Your brain turns it the right way up, and you never notice.

hook: Dogs can catch your yawns.
facts: Yawning spreads between people, even reading about it can make you yawn.
Studies found that dogs often yawn after watching a human yawn.
And they do it more with their owners than with strangers.

hook: Birds cannot feel the heat of chillies.
facts: Chillies make a chemical that burns in the mouths of mammals.
Birds do not have the sensor that feels it.
So birds eat the peppers happily, and spread the seeds far away, just as the plant wants.

hook: Moths remember lessons from when they were caterpillars.
facts: Inside the cocoon, a caterpillar's body turns almost to liquid.
Scientists trained caterpillars to avoid a smell with a tiny shock.
After they became moths, they still avoided that smell.

hook: Penguins have hidden knees.
facts: Penguins look like they waddle on very short legs.
But under their feathers, their legs are folded up.
Their knees are hidden inside the body, so they always look like they are squatting.

hook: Bees dance to give each other directions.
facts: When a bee finds flowers, it flies home to tell the others.
It dances in a figure eight and shakes its body.
The angle shows the direction, and the length of the shake shows the distance.

hook: Pandas have the stomach of a meat eater.
facts: Giant pandas eat almost nothing but bamboo.
But their gut is short and simple, like a meat eater's.
Their body takes in only a small part of what they eat, so they must eat for most of the day.

hook: One shark can live for four hundred years.
facts: The Greenland shark swims very slowly in icy Arctic water.
Scientists studied the lenses of its eyes to find out its age.
The oldest one they found may have been swimming for about four hundred years.

hook: Some ants are farmers.
facts: Leafcutter ants cut pieces of leaves and carry them home.
But they do not eat the leaves.
They use them to grow a fungus garden, and the fungus is their food.

hook: Wild parrots give their babies names.
facts: Scientists studied small green parrots in Venezuela.
Each chick has its own special call that the others use to talk to it.
The parents give the first version of the name, and the chick keeps it for life.

hook: Prairie dogs can describe what you are wearing.
facts: Prairie dogs warn each other with fast alarm calls.
A scientist found that the calls change depending on the danger.
They can even signal the color of a person's shirt, and how tall they are.

hook: Sheep can recognize famous human faces.
facts: Scientists in Cambridge trained sheep with photos of famous people.
The sheep learned to pick out a famous actress on a screen.
They even recognized her from angles they had never seen before.

hook: Antarctica has a waterfall that looks like blood.
facts: In East Antarctica, a red stream flows out of a white glacier.
The water comes from an old salty lake trapped under the ice, full of iron.
When the iron meets the air it rusts, and the ice turns blood red.

hook: Half of your oxygen comes from the ocean.
facts: People thank forests for the air we breathe.
But tiny plants floating in the sea, called plankton, also make oxygen.
They make around half of all the oxygen on Earth.

hook: Some of your water is older than the Sun.
facts: Water formed in the cold clouds of space before our Sun was born.
Scientists studied the type of hydrogen in Earth's oceans.
They found that a large part of it must have survived from before the Sun existed.

hook: The sunlight on your face is ancient.
facts: Light leaves the surface of the Sun and reaches us in about eight minutes.
But that energy was made deep in the center of the Sun.
It bounced around inside for tens of thousands of years before it could escape.

hook: In hot countries, ripe oranges can stay green.
facts: An orange turns orange when the nights get cold.
In tropical countries the nights stay warm, so many ripe oranges stay green.
In some places, oranges are treated with gas just to look orange for buyers.
